chapter.name: Electric Charges and Fields
chapter.blurb: Starting from the sparks and crackles of rubbed objects, this chapter builds electrostatics from two ideas: Coulomb's inverse-square law for the force between point charges and the superposition principle. It introduces the properties of charge, the electric field and its field lines, electric flux and the electric dipole, including the torque on a dipole in a uniform field. It ends with Gauss's law and its use in finding the field of a long charged wire, a plane sheet of charge and a thin spherical shell.

scope_in.item: State that there are two kinds of charge, that like charges repel and unlike charges attract, and apply the sign convention (glass rod rubbed with silk and cat's fur positive; plastic rod rubbed with fur and silk negative); explain neutralisation on contact and the naming of charges as positive and negative
Describe the gold-leaf electroscope and explain why its leaves diverge and what the degree of divergence indicates
Explain charging by rubbing as a transfer of electrons (positive by losing electrons, negative by gaining them), with no new charge created

Distinguish conductors (metals, human and animal bodies, earth) from insulators (glass, porcelain, plastic, nylon, wood); explain how charge spreads over a conductor but stays put on an insulator, and why a hand-held metal object does not stay charged while one with an insulating handle does
Treat small charged bodies as point charges; add charges algebraically as scalars (additivity)
State and apply conservation of charge for an isolated system, including creation of charged particles with zero net charge (neutron to proton plus electron)

State and apply quantisation of charge q = ne with e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C; count electrons transferred; use the coulomb, micro-C and mC; explain why quantisation can be ignored at the macroscopic level (Examples 1.1, 1.2; Exercises 1.4, 1.5, 1.11)

State Coulomb's law in scalar and vector form with k = 1/(4 pi epsilon0) = 9 x 10^9 N m^2/C^2 and epsilon0 = 8.854 x 10^-12 C^2/N m^2; calculate forces between two point charges and use the ratio reasoning for changed charges or distance; relate the law to Newton's third law; describe Coulomb's torsion-balance method and charge sharing between identical spheres (Examples 1.3, 1.4; Exercises 1.1, 1.2, 1.12)
Compare electric and gravitational forces between proton and electron and find the accelerations they produce (Example 1.3; Exercise 1.3)

State the superposition principle and find the net force on a charge due to several charges by vector addition, including symmetric arrangements on a line, a square and an equilateral triangle (Examples 1.5, 1.6; Exercise 1.6)

Define electric field as force per unit positive test charge (E = lim F/q), with unit N/C; use F = qE; give the field of a point charge and its direction and spherical symmetry; distinguish source and test charge
Find the field of a system of point charges by superposition at points on the line of the charges and at symmetric points off the line (Example 1.8; Exercise 1.8)
Explain the physical significance of the field (time delay, speed c, fields as physical entities) qualitatively
Find the force, acceleration and time of travel of a charged particle released from rest in a uniform field, and compare with free fall under gravity (Example 1.7)

Define electric field lines and state their properties (tangent gives direction, density gives relative strength, start on positive and end on negative charges, continuous in charge-free regions, never cross, no closed loops); describe the patterns for single charges, two like charges, a dipole and a uniform field (Exercise 1.7)

Treat an area element as a vector along its normal (outward normal for a closed surface) and calculate electric flux E Delta-S cos theta in N m^2/C through flat surfaces, cubes and cylinders in uniform or simply varying fields (Examples 1.10(a), 1.11(a)-(c); Exercises 1.14, 1.15)

Define an electric dipole and its dipole moment p = q x 2a directed from -q to +q; use the axial and equatorial field expressions, both exact and for r >> a, with their directions and the 1/r^3 dependence (Example 1.9; Exercise 1.9)
Distinguish polar molecules (H2O) from molecules with zero dipole moment (CO2, CH4)

Find the net force (zero) and torque tau = p x E, magnitude pE sin theta, on a dipole in a uniform field; describe qualitatively the net force on a dipole in a non-uniform field and the attraction of paper by a charged comb (Exercise 1.10)

Define linear, surface and volume charge densities with their units and explain their macroscopic meaning; state that the field of a continuous distribution follows from Coulomb's law and superposition

State Gauss's law (flux through a closed surface = q/epsilon0, stated without proof), verify it for a point charge at the centre of a sphere, state the points to note about it, and use it to relate net flux and enclosed charge (Examples 1.10, 1.11; Exercises 1.16-1.19, 1.21)
Derive and use the field of an infinitely long straight uniformly charged wire, E = lambda/(2 pi epsilon0 r) (Exercise 1.22)
Derive and use the field of a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet, E = sigma/(2 epsilon0), including superposing the fields of two parallel sheets (Exercise 1.23)

Derive and use the field of a uniformly charged thin spherical shell outside (as a point charge at the centre) and inside (zero); the same outside result for a uniformly charged sphere (Example 1.12; Exercise 1.20)

concepts.name: Electric charge, conductors and insulators
concepts.description: Two kinds of charge and their polarity, charging by rubbing as a transfer of electrons, detecting charge with a gold-leaf electroscope, and how conductors and insulators hold charge differently.
concepts.idea: Rubbing does not create charge; it moves a few electrons from one body to the other, leaving one body positive and the other negative, and like charges repel while unlike charges attract.
concepts.rule: There are only two kinds of electric charge. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract; the property that tells the two kinds apart is the polarity of charge. By convention the charge on a glass rod rubbed with silk (and on cat's fur) is positive, and the charge on a plastic rod rubbed with fur (and on silk) is negative. A body is charged positively by losing some electrons and negatively by gaining electrons; no new charge is created, and only a very small fraction of the electrons is transferred. Unlike charges neutralise each other's effect when the bodies touch. A gold-leaf electroscope detects charge: charge flows to the two leaves, which diverge, and the degree of divergence indicates the amount of charge. Conductors (metals, human and animal bodies, the earth) let charge move through them and charge given to a conductor spreads over its whole surface; insulators (glass, porcelain, plastic, nylon, wood) do not, and charge put on an insulator stays where it is.
concepts.example: A glass rod rubbed with silk repels another rubbed glass rod but attracts a plastic rod rubbed with fur, because glass is positive and the plastic rod is negative.

concepts.name: Basic properties of charge: additivity, conservation and quantisation
concepts.description: Charges add algebraically like scalars, the total charge of an isolated system is conserved, and every charge is an integral multiple of the basic unit e.
concepts.idea: Charge is a scalar that can be positive or negative, it is never created or destroyed in total, and it comes only in whole-number multiples of e.
concepts.rule: A point charge is a charged body whose size is very small compared with the distances involved. Additivity: the total charge of a system is the algebraic sum of its charges, with proper signs; charge is a scalar like mass, but mass is always positive while charge can be positive or negative. Conservation: the total charge of an isolated system does not change; charge-carrying particles may be created or destroyed (a neutron turns into a proton and an electron) but the net charge stays the same. Quantisation: q = n e, where n is an integer, positive or negative, and e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C is the magnitude of the charge on an electron or proton. A body with n1 electrons and n2 protons has charge (n2 - n1) e. The SI unit of charge is the coulomb (C); 1 micro-C = 10^-6 C and 1 mC = 10^-3 C. At the macroscopic level the step e is so small that charge appears continuous and quantisation can be ignored.
concepts.example: A body that has lost 5 electrons carries a charge of 5 x 1.6 x 10^-19 C = +8.0 x 10^-19 C; a charge of 1.0 x 10^-19 C is impossible because it is not a whole multiple of e.

questions.q: Compose a short explanation, built around an analogy of your own choice, for a younger student who asks: 'If charge comes in lumps of e, why does the charge on a rubbed comb seem to take any value?' s: Suitable analogy of a grainy thing looking continuous

concepts.name: Coulomb's law
concepts.description: The force between two point charges in vacuum: proportional to the product of the charges, inversely proportional to the square of their separation and directed along the line joining them.
concepts.idea: Two point charges push or pull each other along the line joining them with a force that grows with the product of the charges and falls as the square of the distance.
concepts.rule: For two point charges q1 and q2 a distance r apart in vacuum, F = k |q1 q2| / r^2 with k = 1/(4 pi epsilon0), approximately 9 x 10^9 N m^2/C^2; epsilon0 = 8.854 x 10^-12 C^2/N m^2 is the permittivity of free space. In vector form F21 = (1/(4 pi epsilon0)) (q1 q2 / r21^2) r21-hat, where r21-hat is the unit vector from charge 1 to charge 2: like charges give a force along r21-hat (repulsion) and unlike charges a force opposite to it (attraction). F12 = -F21, so the law agrees with Newton's third law. Charged bodies may be treated as point charges only when their sizes are much smaller than their separation. Coulomb measured the force with a torsion balance and obtained charges q/2, q/4, ... by touching a charged sphere to an identical uncharged one. Two charges of 1 C each 1 m apart repel with 9 x 10^9 N, so the coulomb is a very large unit. The electric force between a proton and an electron is about 10^39 times their gravitational force.
concepts.example: Two charges of +1 micro-C and +4 micro-C placed 20 cm apart repel with F = 9 x 10^9 x (1 x 10^-6)(4 x 10^-6)/(0.2)^2 = 0.9 N.

concepts.name: Forces between multiple charges: the superposition principle

concepts.idea: Each pair of charges interacts exactly as Coulomb's law says, as if the others were absent, and the net force on a charge is the vector sum of these pair forces.
concepts.rule: Principle of superposition: the force on any charge due to a number of other charges is the vector sum of all the forces on that charge due to the other charges, taken one at a time; the individual forces are unaffected by the presence of the other charges. F1 = F12 + F13 + ... + F1n, with each term given by Coulomb's law, and the sum found by the parallelogram law of vector addition. All of electrostatics is basically a consequence of Coulomb's law and the superposition principle. For equal charges q at the vertices of an equilateral triangle the net force on a charge at the centroid is zero. For charges q, q and -q at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side l, with F = q^2/(4 pi epsilon0 l^2), the net force on each charge q has magnitude F and on -q it is sqrt(3) F, and the three net forces add to zero.
concepts.example: A charge that feels 6 N towards the east from one charge and 8 N towards the north from another feels a net force of sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = 10 N, not 14 N, because forces add as vectors.

concepts.name: Electric field of point charges and motion of a charge in a uniform field
concepts.description: Electric field as force per unit test charge, the field of a point charge and of a system of charges by superposition, and the force and acceleration of a charge in a uniform field.
concepts.idea: A charge fills the space around it with an electric field; any other charge placed there feels a force equal to its charge times the field at that point.
concepts.rule: The electric field at a point is the force that a unit positive test charge would experience there: E = lim (q -> 0) F/q, and F = qE. Its SI unit is N/C. For a point charge Q, E = (1/(4 pi epsilon0)) Q/r^2, directed radially outward if Q is positive and radially inward if Q is negative; its magnitude depends only on r (spherical symmetry). The charge producing the field is the source charge and the charge that tests it is the test charge; E does not depend on the test charge. For a system of charges the field is the vector sum of the fields due to the individual charges. In a uniform field E a particle of charge q and mass m has acceleration a = qE/m, so starting from rest it covers a distance h in time t = sqrt(2h/a); a heavier particle with the same charge takes longer, unlike free fall under gravity. The field concept becomes physically essential for time-dependent phenomena, because effects travel at most at the speed of light c.
concepts.example: At 10 cm from a point charge of 1 micro-C, E = 9 x 10^9 x 1 x 10^-6/(0.1)^2 = 9 x 10^5 N/C, directed away from the charge.

concepts.idea: A pair of equal and opposite charges a small distance apart has zero total charge but a field that falls off as 1/r^3, and in a uniform field it feels a turning effect but no net force.
concepts.rule: An electric dipole is a pair of equal and opposite point charges q and -q separated by 2a. Its dipole moment p has magnitude q x 2a and points from -q to q; its unit is C m. At a distance r from the centre: on the axis E = (1/(4 pi epsilon0)) 2pr/(r^2 - a^2)^2, which for r >> a becomes 2p/(4 pi epsilon0 r^3), along p; on the equatorial plane E = (1/(4 pi epsilon0)) p/(r^2 + a^2)^(3/2), which for r >> a becomes p/(4 pi epsilon0 r^3), directed opposite to p. The dipole field falls as 1/r^3, not 1/r^2. In a uniform field E the net force on a dipole is zero and the torque is tau = p x E, of magnitude pE sin theta, tending to align p with E; it is zero when p is parallel or antiparallel to E. In a non-uniform field there is a net force: towards increasing field when p is parallel to E, towards decreasing field when p is antiparallel. Molecules such as CO2 and CH4 have zero dipole moment; polar molecules such as H2O have a permanent dipole moment.

concepts.name: Continuous charge distribution and Gauss's law
concepts.description: Linear, surface and volume charge densities, and Gauss's law relating the flux through any closed surface to the total charge enclosed.
concepts.idea: The total electric flux through any closed surface depends only on the net charge inside it: flux = q/epsilon0.
concepts.rule: For continuous distributions: linear charge density lambda = Delta-Q/Delta-l (C/m), surface charge density sigma = Delta-Q/Delta-S (C/m^2), volume charge density rho = Delta-Q/Delta-V (C/m^3); each element is small on the macroscopic scale but contains a very large number of microscopic charged constituents. The field of a continuous distribution is found by summing the Coulomb fields of its elements (superposition). Gauss's law: the electric flux through a closed surface S equals q/epsilon0, where q is the total charge enclosed by S, with epsilon0 = 8.854 x 10^-12 C^2/N m^2. It holds for any closed surface whatever its shape or size; q counts only the charges inside, wherever they are located inside, while the field in the flux is due to all charges, inside and outside. The Gaussian surface must not pass through a discrete charge, but may pass through a continuous charge distribution. The law is most useful when the system has symmetry, and it rests on the inverse-square dependence in Coulomb's law. Zero net flux through a closed surface means the total charge enclosed is zero.
concepts.example: A closed surface enclosing a net charge of 17.7 x 10^-9 C has a total outward flux of (17.7 x 10^-9)/(8.85 x 10^-12) = 2000 N m^2/C, whatever its shape.

questions.q: A point charge q is at the centre of an imaginary sphere of radius r. Starting from Coulomb's law for the field of the charge, find the total flux through the sphere by adding up the flux through its area elements, and analyse why the answer does not depend on r.

Adding over all elements, and noting that every element is at the same distance r, total flux = [q/(4 pi epsilon0 r^2)] x S, where S = 4 pi r^2 is the area of the sphere. Hence flux = q/epsilon0. The field decreases as 1/r^2 while the area increases as r^2, so r cancels and the flux is the same for every radius.

concepts.name: Applications of Gauss's law: line charge, plane sheet and spherical shell
concepts.description: Using symmetry and a suitable Gaussian surface to find the field of an infinitely long charged wire, an infinite plane sheet of charge and a thin spherical shell.
concepts.idea: When the charge distribution is highly symmetric, a well-chosen Gaussian surface turns Gauss's law into a one-line calculation of the field.
concepts.rule: Infinitely long straight wire of uniform linear charge density lambda: E = lambda/(2 pi epsilon0 r), radial (outward for positive lambda, inward for negative), using a cylindrical Gaussian surface; r is the perpendicular distance from the wire. Infinite plane sheet of uniform surface charge density sigma: E = sigma/(2 epsilon0), normal to the sheet, away from it for positive sigma and towards it for negative sigma, and independent of the distance from the sheet; for a large finite sheet this holds approximately in the middle region, away from the ends. Thin spherical shell of radius R and total charge q = 4 pi R^2 sigma: for r > R, E = q/(4 pi epsilon0 r^2), as if all the charge were concentrated at the centre; for r < R, E = 0. The same outside result holds for a solid sphere of uniform volume charge density. Fields of several such distributions add by superposition. Useful values: 1/(4 pi epsilon0) = 9 x 10^9 N m^2/C^2, so 1/(2 pi epsilon0) = 1.8 x 10^10 N m^2/C^2.
concepts.example: A plane sheet with sigma = 35.4 x 10^-9 C/m^2 produces E = (35.4 x 10^-9)/(2 x 8.85 x 10^-12) = 2000 N/C on either side, at any distance.
